newsitem.title: INDIA: Police dig for more victims of India mid-air crash.
newsitem.headline: Police dig for more victims of India mid-air crash.

text.p: India on Thursday prepared a mass funeral for victims of the world's worst mid-air collision while police searching for more bodies probed the debris with sticks.
Authorities said they had identified only 131 of 294 bodies found amid the wreckage from Tuesday's collision between a Saudi Arabia Airlines jumbo jet and a Kazakh cargo plane.
A total of 349 passengers and crew, 312 on the Saudi Boeing 747 jet and 37 on the Ilyushin Il-76 freighter, were killed in India's worst aviation disaster.
"We are hopeful of identifying more bodies," police superintendent Mohammad Akil said in Charkhi Dadri, where the planes fell to the ground, about 80 km (50 miles) west of Delhi.
The Saudi airliner and the incoming Kazakh plane collided seven minutes after the Saudi 747 had taken off from New Delhi at nightfall on Tuesday.

Aviation experts said the cause of the crash could be known in the next two weeks. Indian officials denied that faulty equipment on the ground or misunderstood instructions from the control tower were to blame.
Akil said officials would meet Hindu and Moslem leaders later in the day to decide what to do with unidentifiable bodies and body parts.

"We will hold a meeting this afternoon and decide whether to cremate or bury," he said. Hindus cremate their dead while Moslems bury them. "By today evening or tomorrow morning, we will dispose of the bodies," he said.
Alimmuddin Asadi of the Moslem Jamiat Ulema Hind religious organisation, said many of the victims were Moslems. "We want their last rites to be done according to Islamic ways," he said.
Jet Ram Gupta, district president of the Hindu Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, said local officials would decide what to do with the bodies. "We will not create any disputes," he said.
Authorities said that based on flight manifests, they knew how many passengers were on the planes and their names. But they had not yet released an official list with nationalities.

All 37 victims on the chartered KazAir plane, which was taking businessmen to Delhi to pick up goods, had been identified. A Saudi newspaper said the victims on the Saudi airliner included 215 Indians, 13 Saudis, and three Pakistanis.
Nepal said there were 53 Nepalis on board, most of them headed for jobs as manual labourers, drivers and plumbers. There were three women, two Americans and one Briton aboard, officials said.
Some 59 bodies had been turned over to relatives who had come to the remote, rural region on the northern Indian plain, the Press Trust of India said.

At least 60 bodies were mutilated beyond recognition, and rescuers said more than 50 might be buried in the wreckage of the Saudi airliner, which dug a deep crater in a mustard field when it crashed to the ground.
Bodies were being kept on ice blocks in a nearby hospital. Horse-drawn carriages could be seen taking newly hewn wooden coffins to the hospital.

The army was brought in to help clear the wreckage and search for bodies. But no machinery was seen near the wreckage of the Saudi aircraft early on Thursday, and police used long wooden batons to poke in the debris.

Aviation experts said it could take less than two weeks to ascertain the cause of the collision after searchers recovered the so-called "black boxes", or flight data and cockpit voice recorders, from the wreckage on Wednesday.
Speculation on the cause had ranged from inadequate equipment at New Delhi airport to pilots' misunderstanding of instructions from ground controllers.

Yogesh Chandra, the top civil servant at India's Civil Aviation Ministry, ruled out both. He said the transcript of the final conversations between the pilots and ground control showed both understood their instructions.
The transcript, which Chandra read to reporters, showed the pilots of both aircraft appeared to have understood instructions to maintain altitudes 1,000 feet (300 metres) apart.
Chandra said speculation that ageing equipment at Delhi airport might be to blame was "absolutely incorrect".

But pilots said the government had dragged its feet in installing radar equipment that would have permitted air traffic controllers in Delhi to establish the altitude of both aircraft as well as their direction.
